# The Memory Chess

## A free chess memory game that asks you to study a position, rebuild it from memory, and review your score.

Screenshot of The Memory Chess website

The Memory Chess is a free chess training game designed for players who want to improve board vision, visualization, and spatial memory. Instead of focusing on openings or move calculation, it gives you a position to study briefly, clears the board, and asks you to reconstruct it from memory. You then receive an immediate score showing how accurately you remembered the position. [...] The game works for both beginners and experienced players because the difficulty can be adjusted to match your current recall. You can start with a small number of pieces and more study time, then gradually increase the challenge as your board memory improves. Short rounds also make it easy to fit repeated practice into a regular training routine.

### Key Features

#### Study and Rebuild Positions

The core exercise is simple: study a chess position, let the board clear, and recreate the position from memory.

#### Instant Memory Scoring

Each completed round gives you an immediate result showing how accurately you reconstructed the position.

#### Adjustable Difficulty

The game lets you control how challenging each memory exercise is.

#### Beginner-Friendly Training [...] Because the game is free and doesn't require an account, you can start practicing immediately. An optional leaderboard name lets you record your results publicly if you want to compare scores with other players.

### Train Your Chess Memory One Position at a Time

Study the position, rebuild the board, check your score, and repeat. The Memory Chess provides a simple way to turn visualization and spatial recall into a regular chess training exercise.

## Questions About Memory Chess

What is Memory Chess?

Memory Chess is a free board-memory game. You study a chess position for a short time, rebuild it from memory, and get a score based on how many pieces you placed correctly.

How do I play? [...] How do I play?

Choose how many pieces you want and how long you want to study the board. When the position disappears, place the pieces back on the squares you remember. Submit your answer to see your accuracy and time.

Can beginners play Memory Chess?

Yes. You do not need to know chess openings or calculate moves. Start with fewer pieces and more study time, then make the game harder when you feel ready.

How does it train chess visualization?

Each round gives you focused practice holding a chess position in your mind and recalling where the pieces belong. Your score shows which positions feel easy and where you need more practice.

📈 Chess Improvement Guide

This page is part of the Chess Improvement Guide — A practical roadmap for getting better at chess — diagnose your level, build an effective training routine, and focus on the skills that matter most for your rating.

🧠 Chess Training Tools & Practice Guide [...] How does this chess memory trainer work?

This chess memory trainer shows a position, hides it, and then lets you rebuild the board square by square. That recall cycle exposes whether you remembered piece locations, colours, and relationships accurately. Use the Chess Memory Trainer rebuild board to discover which pieces disappear from your mental picture first.

  How do I start using the chess memory trainer?

You start by choosing a difficulty level, pressing Start Memory Test, studying the position, and rebuilding it after the board is hidden. The important training step is the recall phase, because retrieval strengthens memory more than rereading. Use the difficulty selector above to begin with a piece count you can rebuild calmly. [...] What should I look at first when memorising a position?

You should first look at kings, pawn structure, loose pieces, and piece clusters. These anchors create meaningful chunks, which are easier to remember than disconnected squares. Before the Chess Memory Trainer board disappears, scan those anchors and then rebuild them deliberately.

  Should I memorise squares or patterns in chess?

You should memorise patterns more than individual squares. Strong chess memory is built from chunks such as pawn chains, open files, king shelters, and coordinated pieces. Use the Chess Memory Trainer rebuild board to practise remembering relationships instead of isolated coordinates.

# Memory for chess positions (featuring grandmaster Patrick Wolff)
## Channel: Daniel Simons
45.4K subscribers
778 likes

### Description
106,830 views
Posted: 2012-01-12
Chess grandmaster Patrick Wolff performs a classic chess memory task (filmed by Daniel Simons and Christopher Chabris). We showed him a card depicting a chess position and he then reconstructed the position on a chess board from memory. He makes almost no mistakes for a typical chess position, but has poor memory for a position in which the pieces were randomly positioned. The video illustrates the powerful effect of expertise on pattern perception and memory. This video is ©1998/2011, Daniel J. Simons & Christopher F. Chabris. All rights are reserved.
